verdicts.reason: Both are place/tenure standing claims, but Y gives partial credit to any generic first-person standing claim and counts a concrete owned asset as sufficient, while X requires place/trade-tied identity used independent of data or citation, so specificity-graded and presence-graded scores can diverge.

X requires an ongoing formal relationship (committee seat, permit/grant history, prior filings), whereas Y counts lighter familiarity cues like naming officials or thanking the agency for coordination, which a first-time commenter could display.
One measures the presence of part/section CFR citations, the other a substantive ultra vires legal argument; a comment can cite CFR heavily without contesting authority and vice versa.
Both score self-derived monetary compliance-cost figures with a stated basis, anchored identically at 0 for no numbers.

X credits any job, ownership position, or operational role even with no place or tenure (e.g. a corporate officer), while Y specifically requires tenure/residency or place-and-trade identity, so occupationally positioned but placeless comments split the two.
Both detect prewritten mass-campaign wording versus bespoke individualized prose, and in practice both are read off the same formulaic-language cues in the text.

X credits plain local identity or hands-on operational role with no credentials, while Y requires authority markers such as senior title, licensing, or specialized expertise, so a lifelong resident scores high on X and low on Y.

X measures professional counsel-style register and drafting polish, Y measures precise mapping of the comment to specific docket provisions, CFR sections, and statutory authority; a polished attorney letter with no provision-level mapping separates them.
Both score explicit disclosure of a prior or ongoing dealing with the issuing agency (permits, recurring meetings, prior submissions), with the same zero point of no stated history.

X requires disclosed prior dealings such as permits or recurring meetings, while Y also fires on mere relational politeness like naming officials or thanking the agency, which is available to a first-time commenter.
Both score the same artifact set of email/portal headers, attachment placeholders, filenames, OCR defects, and duplicated cover material against a clean-prose zero point.
Both score whether a concrete, implementable regulatory alternative is specified rather than mere objection, with identical zero points.

Both score the comment's claim to speak for many named organizations or members versus an individual submission; scale signaling and consensus packaging are read off the same member lists and consensus claims.

X rewards dense, disproportionate piling-up of authorities regardless of fit, while Y rewards precise, well-targeted mapping to specific provisions; sloppy citation dumps score high on X and low on Y.
Firsthand operational description and emotional intensity are independent; a calm technical operator account and an outraged content-free rant fall on opposite corners.

Y requires quantified organizational scale, membership, market share, or geographic reach, while X also credits unquantified longevity, assets, facilities, and senior titles, so a prestige-by-titles-and-history comment scores high on X and low on Y.
